e-12398.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
e-12398.problem:
Find the missing limits in the repeated integral below

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \: \textrm{d}V
= 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
\int_{\ast}^{\ast} 
f(x,y,z) \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y
$$

where $R$ is the type II region defined as

$$
R=\left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 4, \: -y^2 \leq z \leq \sqrt{y}, \: -2 \leq x \leq ye^{z+2} \right\}.
$$
e-12398.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z)  \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \: u_1(y,z) \leq x \leq u_2(y,z) \big\}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
\iiint\limits_{R} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm d V = \iint\limits_{D} \left[\int_{u_1(y,z)}^{u_2(y,z)} f(x,y,z)\,\textrm{d}x \right]\,\textrm d A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
u_1(y,z) = -2, \qquad u_2(y,z)  = ye^{z+2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} f(x,y,z) \: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{-2}^{ye^{z+2}} f(x,y,z) \: \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D =\left\{ (x,y) \: : \: 1 \leq y \leq 4, \: -y^2 \leq z \leq \sqrt{y} \right\}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}[{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dz\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{\sqrt{y}}{\int }_{-2}^{y{e}^{z+2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

e-11349.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
\displaystyle \iint\limits_D \left[ \int_{0}^{z} \dfrac{\cos (2y)}{1-y} \,\textrm{d}x \right] \textrm{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D = \left\{ (y,z) \, : \, 0 \leq y \leq \dfrac{\pi}{6}, \: 0 \leq z \leq 2\sqrt{1-y} \right\}.
$$
e-11349.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}[x]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(z-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}{\int }_{0}^{2\sqrt{1-y}}\frac{z\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}{[\frac{{z}^{2}}{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2\sqrt{1-y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)}{1-y}(\frac{4(1-y)}{2}-0)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi /6}2\operatorname{cos}⁡(2y)\,\text{d}y \\  & =[\operatorname{sin}⁡(2y)]_{y=0}^{y=\pi /6} \\  & =\operatorname{sin}⁡(\frac{\pi }{3})-\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

e-11348.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region
e-11348.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 4x^3  \: \mathrm{d}V
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R = \left\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \: 0 \leq x \leq \sqrt{y} \right\},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the $z$-axis, and the line $z = 4-y$ in the first quadrant.
e-11348.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
\displaystyle \iiint \limits_{R} 4x^3 \, \textrm{d}V
= 
\iint\limits_{D} \left[ \int_{0}^{\sqrt{y}} 4x^3 \, \mathrm{d}x \right] \mathrm{d}A.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{y}}4{x}^{3}\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{4}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{y}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{(\sqrt{y})}^{4}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate this double integral over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/3c8712fa0a30ad94f503efe5e080ee89f83eb21f19fba45033bbedeab08ac816.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y}{y}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}[{y}^{2}z]_{z=0}^{z=4-y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}{y}^{2}(4-y)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{4}4{y}^{2}-{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{4}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=4} \\  & =\frac{4}{3}(64-0)-\frac{1}{4}(256-0) \\  & =\frac{64}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

e-12369.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region Given a Diagram
e-12369.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/fc19dd4415663ab027e0fc386d4c5bc81a28c1bc26d5f6cf2083f4f4228a4dea.png)

 

Evaluate the triple integral 
$\displaystyle \iiint\limits_R 12z^2 \: \mathrm{d}V$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
e-12369.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/f25c393f10c35ffd9b4fa91cdf672a516cf6cff974a8aa563d350619a64b79bd.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: (y,z) \in D, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 3-y-z \big\},
$$

where

$$
D = \big\{ (y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1 \big\}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R = \big\{ (x,y,z) \: : \: 0 \leq y \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq z \leq 1, \:\: 0 \leq x \leq 3-y-z \big\}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
\iiint \limits_{R}  12z^2  \: \textrm{d}V 
= 
\int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{3-y-z}  12z^2  \: \mathrm{d}x \: \mathrm{d}z \: \mathrm{d}y.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{3-y-z}12{z}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{3-y-z}12{z}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}12{z}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=3-y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}12{z}^{2}(3-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(36{z}^{2}-12y{z}^{2}-12{z}^{3})\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[12{z}^{3}-4y{z}^{3}-3{z}^{4}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(12-4y-3)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}(9-4y)\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y{:}$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}(9-4y)\,dy & =[9y-2{y}^{2}]_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(9-2)-0 \\  & =7\end{aligned}
$$

The triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz
$$

is defined over the type II region $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,-8\le y\le {sin}^{2}⁡z,\,0\le z\le \pi ,\,-2y-1\le x\le {y}^{2}+2z}.
$$

What is $a+b?$
after.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/a905e1f60fb0aa865c071fcbccbfecb30dcac7a74b4b647d24a40f4c89ff1935.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-2y-1,\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={y}^{2}+2z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-8\le y\le {sin}^{2}⁡z,\,0\le z\le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-8}^{{sin}^{2}⁡z}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dy\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-8}^{{sin}^{2}⁡z}{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=0+\pi =\pi .

The triple integral ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∫ab∫∗∗∫∗∗f(x,y,z)dxdydz is defined over the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):−8≤y≤sin2⁡z,0≤z≤π,−2y−1≤x≤y2+2z}. What is a+b?

a
sin2⁡z+π−8
b
sin2⁡z−8
c
y2+2z−2y−1
d
y2+2z−2y
e
π
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have

u1(y,z)=−2y−1,u2(y,z)=y2+2z.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dA.

Now, the region D is given by D={(x,y):−8≤y≤sin2⁡z,0≤z≤π}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get ∬D[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dA=∫0π∫−8sin2⁡z[∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dx]dydz=∫0π∫−8sin2⁡z∫−2y−1y2+2zf(x,y,z)dxdydz.

Finally, a+b=0+π=π.

content.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
content.problem:
The triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz
$$

is defined over the type II region $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,-8\le y\le {sin}^{2}⁡z,\,0\le z\le \pi ,\,-2y-1\le x\le {y}^{2}+2z}.
$$

What is $a+b?$
content.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/a905e1f60fb0aa865c071fcbccbfecb30dcac7a74b4b647d24a40f4c89ff1935.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-2y-1,\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={y}^{2}+2z.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-8\le y\le {sin}^{2}⁡z,\,0\le z\le \pi }.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-8}^{{sin}^{2}⁡z}[{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dy\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{\pi }{\int }_{-8}^{{sin}^{2}⁡z}{\int }_{-2y-1}^{{y}^{2}+2z}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=0+\pi =\pi .
$$

after.html:
Question 2
?

The triple integral ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∫∗∗∫ab∫∗∗f(x,y,z)dxdzdy is defined over the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):1≤y≤4,2y≤z≤8,0≤x≤z2−y2}. What is a+b?

a
2y+8
b
3
c
z2−y2
d
5
e
2y+3
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows:

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have

u1(y,z)=0,u2(y,z)=z2−y2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫0z2−y2f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

Now, the region D is given by D={(x,y):1≤y≤4,2y≤z≤8}.

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over D as a repeated integral, we get ∬D[∫0z2−y2f(x,y,z)dx]dA=∫14∫2y8[∫0z2−y2f(x,y,z)dx]dzdy=∫14∫2y8∫0z2−y2f(x,y,z)dxdzdy.

Finally, a+b=2y+8.

verification.explanation: The revealed solution confirms that the middle integral, with respect to z, has limits a = 2y and b = 8. Thus a + b = 2y + 8, option a. The observed incorrect submission selected option e, 2y + 3.

content.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
content.problem:
The triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={\int }_{∗}^{∗}{\int }_{a}^{b}{\int }_{∗}^{∗}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dz\,dy
$$

is defined over the type II region $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 4,\,2y\le z\le 8,\,0\le x\le {z}^{2}-{y}^{2}}.
$$

What is $a+b?$
content.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/a905e1f60fb0aa865c071fcbccbfecb30dcac7a74b4b647d24a40f4c89ff1935.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=0,\,{u}_{2}(y,z)={z}^{2}-{y}^{2}.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}-{y}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,1\le y\le 4,\,2y\le z\le 8}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}-{y}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{2y}^{8}[{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}-{y}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dz\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{4}{\int }_{2y}^{8}{\int }_{0}^{{z}^{2}-{y}^{2}}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dz\,dy.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=2y+8.
$$

decision.explanation: For each fixed (y,z) in D, x ranges from -3 to 5y^4+2. Integrate first with respect to x over those bounds, then over D with respect to area.

after.name: Question 3
after.problem:
Consider the type II region $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,-3\le x\le 5{y}^{4}+2},
$$

where $D$ is some finite region in the $yz$-plane. Then,

$$
after.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-3\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=5{y}^{4}+2.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-3}^{5{y}^{4}+2}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Question 3
?

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,−3≤x≤5y4+2}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dz]dA
b
∫−35y4+2[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
c
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dy]dA
d
∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dx]dA
e
∫−35y4+2[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dz
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=−3u2(y,z)=5y4+2.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫−35y4+2f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

content.knowledge_point: Representing a Triple Integral as a Mixed or Repeated Integral
content.problem:
Consider the type II region $R,$ given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,-3\le x\le 5{y}^{4}+2},
$$

where $D$ is some finite region in the $yz$-plane. Then,

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V=
$$
content.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-3\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=5{y}^{4}+2.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-3}^{5{y}^{4}+2}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

after.worked_solution:
A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/a905e1f60fb0aa865c071fcbccbfecb30dcac7a74b4b647d24a40f4c89ff1935.png)

$$

$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=-\sqrt{y+z},\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=4.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-\sqrt{y+z}}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Now, the region $D$ is given by

$$
D={(x,y)\,:\,-z\le y\le 1,\,4\le z\le 5}.
$$

Therefore, by expressing the double integral over $D$ as a repeated integral, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{-\sqrt{y+z}}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA & ={\int }_{4}^{5}{\int }_{-z}^{1}[{\int }_{-\sqrt{y+z}}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dy\,\text{d}z \\  & ={\int }_{4}^{5}{\int }_{-z}^{1}{\int }_{-\sqrt{y+z}}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx\,dy\,dz.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
a+b=4+5=9.
$$

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,yz≤x≤4}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫yz4[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
b
∬D[∫yz4f(x,y,z)dz]dA
c
∬D[∫yz4f(x,y,z)dx]dA
d
∬D[∫yz4f(x,y,z)dy]dA
e
∫yz4[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dy

decision.explanation: For each fixed (y,z) in D, integrate with respect to x from yz to 4, then integrate over D. This gives option c.

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/1b49704bf6d5837a18d8b5dbb8b420d430d5e3881507540fb62a45cf1f6ce52f.png)

 

If $R$ is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ as a mixed integral, as follows:

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\,\text{d}A
$$

In our case, we have

$$
{u}_{1}(y,z)=yz\,{u}_{2}(y,z)=4.
$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{yz}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

Consider the type II region R, given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,yz≤x≤4}, where D is some finite region in the yz-plane. Then, ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=

a
∫yz4[∬Df(x,y,z)dA]dx
b
∬D[∫yz4f(x,y,z)dz]dA

Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

A type II region in three-dimensional space can be written as R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,u1(y,z)≤x≤u2(y,z)}.

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

If R is a type II region, we can express the triple integral of f(x,y,z) over R as a mixed integral, as follows: ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA

In our case, we have u1(y,z)=yzu2(y,z)=4.

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as ∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫yz4f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

content.worked_solution:

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,{u}_{1}(y,z)\le x\le {u}_{2}(y,z)}.
$$

A typical three-dimensional type II region can be visualized schematically, as shown below.

$$

Therefore, our triple integral can be written as

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{yz}^{4}f(x,y,z)\,dx]dA.
$$

after.name: Question 6
after.problem:
Evaluate the mixed integral

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y}12z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A
$$

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le 4-{y}^{2}}.
$$
after.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y}12z\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}12z[x]_{x=0}^{x=y}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12z(y-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}12yz\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}yz\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{4-{y}^{2}}12yz\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6y[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=4-{y}^{2}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}6y(4-{y}^{2})^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(96y-48{y}^{3}+6{y}^{5})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[48{y}^{2}-12{y}^{4}+{y}^{6}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =48(2)^{2}-12(2)^{4}+(2)^{6} \\  & =64\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z}4xz\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}[2z{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=z}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2z({z}^{2}-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{4-2y}}2{z}^{3}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[\frac{1}{2}{z}^{4}]}_{z=0}^{z=\sqrt{4-2y}}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(\sqrt{4-2y)})^{4}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(4-2y)^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}\frac{1}{2}(16-16y+4{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}8-8y+2{y}^{2}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={[8y-4{y}^{2}+\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =16-16+\frac{16}{3} \\  & =\frac{16}{3}\end{aligned}

after.problem:

$$
{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2z}}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A

where the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane is given by

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,1\le y\le 3,\,y\le z\le y+1}.

after.worked_solution:
First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{2z}}\frac{x}{2}\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{4}[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=\sqrt{2z}}\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{4}(2z-0)\,\text{d}A \\  & ={∬}_{D}\frac{1}{2}z\,\text{d}A\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the double integral:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{1}{2}z\,\text{d}A & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{y}^{y+1}\frac{1}{2}z\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{4}[{z}^{2}]_{z=y}^{z=y+1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{4}((y+1)^{2}-{y}^{2})\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{4}(2y+1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{[{y}^{2}+y]}_{y=1}^{y=3} \\  & =\frac{1}{4}(9+3)-\frac{1}{4}(1+1) \\  & =\frac{5}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

after.name: Question 11
after.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}2+2{e}^{x}\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type II region given by 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le y\le 0,\,0\le z\le 1,\,-z\le x\le 0}.
$$
after.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2+2{e}^{x}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-z}^{0}2+2{e}^{x}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-z}^{0}2+2{e}^{x}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{-z}^{0}2+2{e}^{x}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[2x+2{e}^{x}]_{x=-z}^{x=0}dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}0+2{e}^{0}-2(-z)-2{e}^{-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+2z-2{e}^{-z}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z,$ treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+2z-2{e}^{-z}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[{\int }_{0}^{1}2+2z-2{e}^{-z}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{[2z+{z}^{2}+2{e}^{-z}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(2+1+2{e}^{-1})-2{e}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}1+2{e}^{-1}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}1+2{e}^{-1}\,dy & =(1+2{e}^{-1})[y]_{y=-1}^{y=0} \\  & =(1+2{e}^{-1})(0-(-1)) \\  & =2{e}^{-1}+1\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region
content.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral

$$
{∭}_{R}2+2{e}^{x}\,\text{d}V
$$

where $R$ is the type II region given by 

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,-1\le y\le 0,\,0\le z\le 1,\,-z\le x\le 0}.
$$
content.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2+2{e}^{x}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-z}^{0}2+2{e}^{x}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-z}^{0}2+2{e}^{x}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{-z}^{0}2+2{e}^{x}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}[2x+2{e}^{x}]_{x=-z}^{x=0}dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}0+2{e}^{0}-2(-z)-2{e}^{-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+2z-2{e}^{-z}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z,$ treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}{\int }_{0}^{1}2+2z-2{e}^{-z}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}[{\int }_{0}^{1}2+2z-2{e}^{-z}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}{[2z+{z}^{2}+2{e}^{-z}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}(2+1+2{e}^{-1})-2{e}^{0}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{-1}^{0}1+2{e}^{-1}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{-1}^{0}1+2{e}^{-1}\,dy & =(1+2{e}^{-1})[y]_{y=-1}^{y=0} \\  & =(1+2{e}^{-1})(0-(-1)) \\  & =2{e}^{-1}+1\end{aligned}
$$

before.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1},

decision.explanation: In the fourth quadrant, D has bounds 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 and −y² ≤ z ≤ 0. Integrating in x gives y²+z²+1, so the volume is ∫₀¹ ∫₋ᵧ²⁰ (y²+z²+1) dz dy = ∫₀¹ (y⁴+y²+y⁶/3) dy = 1/5+1/3+1/21 = 61/105.

after.name: Question 12
after.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le {y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the parabola $z=-{y}^{2}$ in the fourth quadrant.
after.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[x]_{x=0}^{x={y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/38ea49a6fae41574107b2ba68a578586a306cf43d419d4de5699dcfa009137c2.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{0}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{-{y}^{2}}^{0}{y}^{2}+{z}^{2}+1\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[({y}^{2}+1)z+\frac{1}{3}{z}^{3}]}_{z=-{y}^{2}}^{z=0}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+1)((0-(-{y}^{2}))+\frac{1}{3}(0-{(-{y}^{2})}^{3})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{2}+1){y}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{6}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{4}+{y}^{2}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{6}\,dy \\  & ={[\frac{1}{5}{y}^{5}+\frac{1}{3}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{21}{y}^{7}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{5}+\frac{1}{3}+\frac{1}{21} \\  & =\frac{61}{105}\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the triple integral

∭R2ydV

where the region R is given by R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,0≤x≤z3}, and D is a finite region in yz-plane enclosed between the y-axes, the line y=2 and the line z=y in the first quadrant.

a
12
b
6
c
53
d
43
e
3
Submit

decision.explanation: The region D has bounds 0 ≤ y ≤ 2 and 0 ≤ z ≤ y. Integrating in x gives 2yz√3, then integrating in z gives √3 y³. Thus the integral is √3∫₀² y³ dy = 4√3.

after.name: Question 13
after.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2y\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le z\sqrt{3}},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axes, the line $y=2$ and the line $z=y$ in the first quadrant.
after.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z\sqrt{3}}2y\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z\sqrt{3}}2y\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}2y[x]_{x=0}^{x=z\sqrt{3}}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/63a8768b2769fad339ba7667357812d2dda0ea856e846ad666a100f8bc1336e9.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{y}2yz\sqrt{3}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}[{\int }_{0}^{y}2z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}[{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}y\sqrt{3}({y}^{2}-0)\,dy \\  & =\sqrt{3}{\int }_{0}^{2}{y}^{3}\,dy \\  & =\sqrt{3}{[\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =\sqrt{3}(\frac{16}{4}-0) \\  & =4\sqrt{3}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
{∭}_{R}2y\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le z\sqrt{3}},

{∭}_{R}2y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{z\sqrt{3}}2y\,dx]dA.

$$

after.name: Question 14
after.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le y+z+2},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the $z$-axis and the line $z=2-y$ in the first quadrant.
after.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z+2}y\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z+2}y\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}y[x]_{x=0}^{x=y+z+2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}y(y+z+2)\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/b473cc75dbbd6fa36ba43f6bbdec4a0133164e6fd8bc5f76ff86cec74714a256.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-y}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2-y}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[({y}^{2}+2y)z+\frac{1}{2}y{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2-y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+2y)(2-y)+\frac{1}{2}y(2-y)^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4y-{y}^{3})+\frac{1}{2}y(4-4y+{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}-2{y}^{2}+6y\,dy \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{8}{y}^{4}-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =-2-\frac{16}{3}+12 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region
content.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le y+z+2},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the $z$-axis and the line $z=2-y$ in the first quadrant.
content.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}y\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z+2}y\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{y+z+2}y\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}y[x]_{x=0}^{x=y+z+2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}y(y+z+2)\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/b473cc75dbbd6fa36ba43f6bbdec4a0133164e6fd8bc5f76ff86cec74714a256.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{2-y}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{2-y}{y}^{2}+yz+2y\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{[({y}^{2}+2y)z+\frac{1}{2}y{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=2-y}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}({y}^{2}+2y)(2-y)+\frac{1}{2}y(2-y)^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(4y-{y}^{3})+\frac{1}{2}y(4-4y+{y}^{2})\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}-2{y}^{2}+6y\,dy \\  & ={[-\frac{1}{8}{y}^{4}-\frac{2}{3}{y}^{3}+3{y}^{2}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =-2-\frac{16}{3}+12 \\  & =\frac{14}{3}\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: D has bounds 0 ≤ y ≤ 1 and 0 ≤ z ≤ y². Integrating 2x from 0 to yz gives y²z². Therefore the integral is ∫₀¹ ∫₀^{y²} y²z² dz dy = ∫₀¹ y⁸/3 dy = 1/27.

after.name: Question 15
after.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le yz},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the parabola $z={y}^{2}$ in the first quadrant.
after.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{yz}2x\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{yz}2x\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=yz}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}(yz)^{2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/acb173db9d28ed8b38e63c7bc365c20e5755aeb1af3f6340e7b9229a4b49101d.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z={y}^{2}}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}({y}^{6}-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{8}\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{1}{9}{y}^{9}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{9}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Evaluating a Triple Integral Over a Type II Region
content.problem:
Evaluate the triple integral 

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,dV
$$

where the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,0\le x\le yz},
$$

and $D$ is a finite region in $yz$-plane enclosed between the $y$-axis, the line $y=1$ and the parabola $z={y}^{2}$ in the first quadrant.
content.worked_solution:
Writing down our triple integral as a mixed integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{yz}2x\,dx]dA.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x,$ treating $y$ and $z$ as constants:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}[{\int }_{0}^{yz}2x\,dx]dA & ={∬}_{D}[{x}^{2}]_{x=0}^{x=yz}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}(yz)^{2}\,dA \\  & ={∬}_{D}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dA\end{aligned}
$$

We must now evaluate the double integral above over the region $D$ in the $yz$-plane shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/acb173db9d28ed8b38e63c7bc365c20e5755aeb1af3f6340e7b9229a4b49101d.png)

We can evaluate our double integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dA & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{{y}^{2}}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}{z}^{3}]}_{z=0}^{z={y}^{2}}dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{2}({y}^{6}-0)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{1}{3}{y}^{8}\,dy \\  & =\frac{1}{3}{[\frac{1}{9}{y}^{9}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{3}(\frac{1}{9}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{27}\end{aligned}
$$

${∭}_{R}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/0008ba406cfe8a5b61d683a6854260897cb441752a5333add281ab1279e31b0b.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2-\frac{y}{3}+z},
$$

where

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 3}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/bbe6b6b897e5d53421080ae8e8b9dc49f2ea1b7e135f8426ee3f11af01cc2401.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 3,\,\,0\le z\le 3,\,\,0\le 2-\frac{y}{3}+z}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{2-y/3+z}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2-y/3+z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{6-y+3z}(2-\frac{y}{3}+z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{3}[{\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}{[z]}_{z=0}^{z=3}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\frac{1}{3}(3)\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{3}\,dy & =[y]_{y=0}^{y=3} \\  & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/2427e053c0e2d808b32db5d7fedf81365e7e50f0b3f2dc61598ad1795394686e.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z},
$$

where

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/145f0d494ffe24de84e3a289b3a7316d3f4933f193d734aed118609f7fb9f94f.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 1,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 2+2y-z}
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}{y}^{2}\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{2+2y-z}{y}^{2}\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}[x]_{x=0}^{x=2+2y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{2}(2+2y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-{y}^{2}z\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{[2{y}^{2}z+2{y}^{3}z-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}{z}^{2}]}_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}2{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}-\frac{1}{2}{y}^{2}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{1}\frac{3}{2}{y}^{2}+2{y}^{3}\,dy & ={[\frac{1}{2}{y}^{3}+\frac{1}{2}{y}^{4}]}_{y=0}^{y=1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{2})-0 \\  & =1.\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,0≤x≤2+2y−z},

where

D={(y,z):0≤y≤1,0≤z≤1}

is the projection of R onto the yz-plane, shown below.

Hence, we can express the region R as

R={(x,y,z):0≤y≤1,0≤z≤1,0≤x≤2+2y−z}

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

∭Ry2dV=∫01∫01∫02+2y−zy2dxdzdy.

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to x, treating y and z as constants:

∫01∫01∫02+2y−zy2dxdzdy=∫01∫01[∫02+2y−zy2dx]dzdy=∫01∫01y2[x]x=0x=2+2y−zdzdy=∫01∫01y2(2+2y−z)dzdy=∫01∫012y2+2y3−y2zdzdy

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to z, treating y as a constant:

∫01∫012y2+2y3−y2zdzdy=∫01[∫012y2+2y3−y2zdz]dy=∫01[2y2z+2y3z−12y2z2]z=0z=1dy=∫012y2+2y3−12y2dy=∫0132y2+2y3dy

Finally, we integrate with respect to y:

∫0132y2+2y3dy=[12y3+12y4]y=0y=1=(12+12)−0=1.

verification.explanation: The worked solution confirms the bounds 0 ≤ y,z ≤ 1 and 0 ≤ x ≤ 2+2y−z. Integrating in x and z gives ∫₀¹ ((3/2)y²+2y³) dy = 1/2+1/2 = 1, so option a is correct.

Evaluate the triple integral 
${∭}_{R}4y\,dV$
over the region $R,$ shown above.

*Hint: All surfaces, except for the front one, are parallel to the corresponding coordinate planes.*
after.worked_solution:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/9bb9311cbaf796f76c4b8b7cb7ed81abec48abc445b894f838f940fbd92e534b.png)

 

Notice that our solid can be written as the type II region

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y-z},
$$

where

$$
D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1}
$$

is the projection of $R$ onto the $yz$-plane, shown below.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/82f237dc5fb7d8b8ed34b7a1c16527ab338923a33462f0bd7dafbe54bc5e5158.png)

Hence, we can express the region $R$ as

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,\,0\le z\le 1,\,\,0\le x\le 4-y-z}.
$$

As a result, by writing down our triple integral as a repeated integral, we obtain

$$
{∭}_{R}4y\,\text{d}V={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}4y\,dx\,dz\,dy.
$$

First, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $x$, treating $y$ and $z$ as constants: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}4y\,dx\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}[{\int }_{0}^{4-y-z}4y\,dx]dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4y[x]_{x=0}^{x=4-y-z}\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}4y(4-y-z)\,dz\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(16y-4{y}^{2}-4yz)\,dz\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we evaluate the inner integral with respect to $z$, treating $y$ as a constant: 

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{1}(16y-4{y}^{2}-4yz)\,dz\,dy & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[{\int }_{0}^{1}(16y-4{y}^{2}-4yz)\,dz]dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}[16yz-4{y}^{2}z-2y{z}^{2}]_{z=0}^{z=1}\,dy \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}(14y-4{y}^{2})\,dy\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we integrate with respect to $y:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{0}^{2}(14y-4{y}^{2})\,dy & ={[7{y}^{2}-\frac{4}{3}{y}^{3}]}_{y=0}^{y=2} \\  & =(28-\frac{32}{3})-0 \\  & =\frac{52}{3}.\end{aligned}
$$

decision.explanation: The solid has 1 ≤ x ≤ 2 and projects onto the upper semicircle (y−1)²+z² ≤ 1, z ≥ 0. Integrating 2x in x gives [x²]₁² = 3. The projection has bounds 0 ≤ y ≤ 2 and 0 ≤ z ≤ √(1−(y−1)²), giving option a.

after.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/f1f3493cd1ff0bee115bf7c311504a2b8a9bbd38dd35adae96c9f7abcae40ae1.png)

Given that $R$ is the type II region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V=$
after.worked_solution:
For a type II region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/6cc327f63d7141c43852e868812a7cff1ec9ae0acfed636ff896ceb204b6fbf0.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
(y-1)^{2}+{z}^{2}=1\,⟺\,z=\sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/a0fb19d32c2545e5c2a61cbb54536e7c28b1a54dbce51c7752c3687035d6c3d6.png)

Hence, $D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}}[{x}^{2}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}}3\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$

EXPLANATION

For a type II region R with projection D onto the yz-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function f(x,y,z) over R is given by

∭Rf(x,y,z)dV=∬D[∫u1(y,z)u2(y,z)f(x,y,z)dx]dA.

We consider the region R as a type II region enclosed between the back surface x=u1(y,z)=1 and the front surface x=u2(y,z)=2.

So, the region R is given by

R={(x,y,z):(y,z)∈D,1≤x≤2}.

Now, we consider the projection D as a type I plane region in the yz-plane with the upper curve

(y−1)2+z2=1⟺z=1−(y−1)2.

Hence, D={(y,z):0≤y≤2,0≤z≤1−(y−1)2}.

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

∭R2xdV=∬D[∫122xdx]dA=∫02∫01−(y−1)2[∫122xdx]dzdy=∫02∫01−(y−1)2[x2]x=1x=2dzdy=∫02∫01−(y−1)23dzdy

content.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/f1f3493cd1ff0bee115bf7c311504a2b8a9bbd38dd35adae96c9f7abcae40ae1.png)

Given that $R$ is the type II region shown above, 
${∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V=$
content.worked_solution:
For a type II region $R$ with projection $D$ onto the $yz$-plane, the triple integral of a continuous function $f(x,y,z)$ over $R$ is given by

$$
{∭}_{R}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}V={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{{u}_{1}(y,z)}^{{u}_{2}(y,z)}f(x,y,z)\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A.
$$

We consider the region $R$ as a type II region enclosed between the back surface $x={u}_{1}(y,z)=1$ and the front surface $x={u}_{2}(y,z)=2.$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/6cc327f63d7141c43852e868812a7cff1ec9ae0acfed636ff896ceb204b6fbf0.png)

So, the region $R$ is given by

$$
R={(x,y,z)\,:\,(y,z)\in D,\,1\le x\le 2}.
$$

Now, we consider the projection $D$ as a type I *plane* region in the $yz$-plane with the upper curve

$$
(y-1)^{2}+{z}^{2}=1\,⟺\,z=\sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}.
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14063435/assets/a0fb19d32c2545e5c2a61cbb54536e7c28b1a54dbce51c7752c3687035d6c3d6.png)

Hence, $D={(y,z)\,:\,0\le y\le 2,\,0\le z\le \sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}}.$

Therefore, we write the triple integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{∭}_{R}2x\,\text{d}V & ={∬}_{D}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}A \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}}[{\int }_{1}^{2}2x\,\text{d}x]\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}}[{x}^{2}]_{x=1}^{x=2}\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2}{\int }_{0}^{\sqrt{1-(y-1)^{2}}}3\,\text{d}z\,\text{d}y\end{aligned}
$$
